<details class="talk" id="user-2026">
<summary><h2>useR! 2026: Visual Explanations of XAI Explainers</h2></summary>

LIME, SHAP, counterfactuals and Anchors often give conflicting explanations for the same prediction, because each looks at a different facet of the model. Using a wombat loan-eligibility example, this talk splits these methods into three shared parts: a perturbation mechanism, an optimisation objective and a structured output. It then shows geometric representations that place each explanation back in the data space. It also introduces two of my R packages: [kumquat](https://janithwanni.github.io/kumquat/), for inspecting LIME's internals, and [kultarr](https://janithwanni.github.io/kultarr/), an Anchors implementation in pure R.

<div class = "talk-links">

[Slides & code](https://github.com/janithwanni/user-2026)

</div>

</details>

<details class="talk" id="numbats-quarto-tutorial-2025">
<summary><h2>NUMBATs Tutorial 2025: Engaging Reproducible Presentations</h2></summary>

In July 2025, Krisanat Anukarnsakulchularp, Jayani Lakshika and I ran a three-part [NUMBATs](https://numbat.space) workshop on reproducibility with Quarto, mentored by Professor Di Cook. I led the third session, on building presentations with Quarto and reveal.js. Starting from a basic `.qmd` file, it covers adding and positioning images with alt text, showing code and output with animated transitions, built-in and custom SCSS themes, design choices for accessibility, presentation tools such as speaker view and overview mode, incremental animations, and hosting the slides as static HTML.

<div class = "talk-links">

[Slides](https://numbat-tutorials.github.io/tutorial_reproducibility_with_quarto/session3/#/)
[Workshop](https://numbat-tutorials.github.io/tutorial_reproducibility_with_quarto/)
[GitHub](https://github.com/numbat-tutorials/tutorial_reproducibility_with_quarto)

</div>

</details>

<details class="talk" id="hacky-hour-ojs-2024">
<summary><h2>NUMBATs Hacky Hour 2024: Fun with ObservableJS</h2></summary>

A short walkthrough for R users on using ObservableJS (OJS) inside Quarto, given at the Hacky Hour of the [NUMBATs](https://numbat.space) group at Monash on 7 March 2024. Starting from the palmer penguins data, it shows how to pass data from R to OJS with `ojs_define()`, build a faceted scatterplot with Observable Plot and compare it to ggplot2, and then add interactivity with Observable Inputs. It all runs in the browser, so there's no Shiny server needed.

<div class = "talk-links">

[Document](https://janithwanni.quarto.pub/fun-with-ojs/)
[GitHub](https://github.com/janithwanni/fun-with-ojs)

</div>

</details>

<details class="talk" id="iasc-ars-2023">
<summary><h2>IASC-ARS 2023: Seeing the Smoke Before the Fire</h2></summary>

This talk was given at the 12th conference of the Asian Regional Section of the International Association for Statistical Computing at Macquarie University, Sydney. It applied counterfactual explanations and Anchors to machine learning models of bushfires, to show the spatiotemporal indicators that push a prediction towards fire. The talk received the **Outstanding Young Researcher / Student Contributed Oral Presentation Award**.

</details>

<details class="talk" id="hacky-hour-webr-2023">
<summary><h2>NUMBATs Hacky Hour 2023: webR</h2></summary>

An introduction to webR, which runs R entirely in a web browser, given at the Hacky Hour of the [NUMBATs](https://numbat.space) group at Monash on 6 September 2023. The talk follows John, a student who turns up to a tutorial with only a tablet. It covers managing files, installing packages, wrangling data and making plots (including sf maps) in the webR REPL. It then explains how webR differs from Shiny.

</details>

<details class="talk" id="user-2022">
<summary><h2>useR! 2022: scatteR</h2></summary>

I presented scatteR in the Synthetic Data and Text Analysis session as a diversity scholarship winner, and chaired the Inference Methods session. scatteR generates scatterplots that match target scagnostic measures, giving controllable data for testing visual and machine learning methods.

<details class="talk" id="rladiescolombo-april-2021-meetup">
<summary><h2>RLadiesColombo April 2021 meetup</h2></summary>

<img src="img/talks/RLadies_poster.webp" width="676" height="380" alt="" class = "talks-img">

The RLadies initiative interested me from the beginning when I was introduced to it on the very first lecture with [Dr. Thiyanga Talagala](https://thiyanga.netlify.app/). Even though I was scared to engage with the community as my initial thought was that I would not be welcome there, I joined my first RLadies meetup with the Plot a lot with ggplot2 workshop done by Priyanga and Thiyanga Talagala. After a few months, I myself received the opportunity to present my knowledge on Data Wrangling in R at the April Meetup of RLadies Colombo. 

The idea that I wanted to follow in this session was to stray away from the standard workshop format of introducing several functions in a specific package and instead wanted to give a real life scenario where these functions will be used. I had a firm belief that people tend to learn things when they use it in a practical context that means something to them. Hence I used the idea of asking the audience to imagine that they are an intern at Spotify and that they are assigned different tasks that require the specific use of a data wrangling function in the dplyr,tidyr and lubridate packages.

<details class="talk" id="tensorflow-all-around-2019">
<summary><h2>Tensorflow All Around 2019</h2></summary>

Tensorflow All Around was an event organized by the Tensorflow User Group of Sri Lanka parallel to similar events organized all through out the globe. I was the head of the Tensorflow User Group of Sri Lanka during this period and I took the initiative to organize the event and presented a talk on using Tensorflow.js for sentiment analysis on the browser. There were over 30 participants who followed along with the talk by trying out the different components of setting up Tensorflow.js on a webpage and classifying sentiment of text collected through an API call with the help of a Universal Sentence Encoder.

<details class="talk" id="fundamentals-of-data-visualization">
<summary><h2>Fundamentals of Data Visualization</h2></summary>

During my time as the President of the Statistics Society, I decided to initiate a data visualization competition called Pearl Viz. The inspiration for the name came from Iron Viz, the annual data visualization competition organized by Tableau and since Sri Lanka is known as the Pearl of the Indian Ocean. Data visualization is a skill that most statistics undergraduates obtain in their first year in the university. However, the tools that were used for data visualization in the classroom was limited by their performance and sharing capabilities. Therefore new visualization technologies should be introduced if the students were to take on the task of providing visualizations using modern Business Intelligence tools. To introduce students to these tools along with the Do's and Dont's of data visualization, I organized a short webinar on the Fundamentals of Data Visualization. As a live demo I took a wireframe sketch of a dashboard based on the career of the popular pop artist P!nk and turned it into a shareable interactive web based dashboard using Google Data Studio.

<details class="talk" id="data-visualization-in-tableau">
<summary><h2>Data Visualization in Tableau</h2></summary>

As the next step of preparing students to modern BI tools, I decided to give a small tutorial on Tableau, specifically Tableau Public and Tableau Cloud, two free data visualization tools that undergraduates can use to learn and enhance their skills to be better prepared for the industry. In this instance a live demo was done using the starter demo dataset from Tableau on the amount of $\text{CO}_2$ emmisions while another live demo was done using an movie profit and review dataset.
